Pin 1 — When Should You Start Pumping?
Wondering when to start pumping if you're breastfeeding? 🤱
The answer isn't the same for every mom. If you're exclusively breastfeeding, you may not need to pump right away. Introducing a bottle around 4 weeks and starting with small pumping sessions can help make the transition smoother—for both you and your baby.
📌 Save this pin for when you're ready to start pumping.
🎥 Watch the full expert video on the Momcozy YouTube channel for more evidence-based breastfeeding guidance from IBCLC Michelle Anthonio.
#Momcozy #BeACozyMom #Breastfeeding #PumpingTips #IBCLC #NewMom #BreastfeedingSupport
Pin 2 — When Is Earlier Pumping Needed?
Sometimes pumping needs to start earlier—and that's completely normal.
If your baby isn't nursing well, you're separated from your baby, or you're combination feeding, pumping can help protect your milk supply by keeping milk moving.
📌 Save this guide so you'll know when pumping may be helpful.
🎥 Learn more in the full Momcozy Care Program episode on YouTube, where IBCLC Michelle Anthonio explains different pumping scenarios in detail.
#Momcozy #BeACozyMom #Breastfeeding #ExclusivePumping #MilkSupply #IBCLC #PostpartumSupport
Pin 3 — Build a Milk Stash Without Oversupply
You don't need a freezer full of milk to be successful.
Building a milk stash slowly can help avoid oversupply while giving you enough milk for future bottle feeds. Small, consistent pumping sessions often work better than aggressive pumping.
📌 Save these tips for your breastfeeding journey.
🎥 Watch the full YouTube episode to learn how to create a pumping plan that fits your family's needs.
#Momcozy #BeACozyMom #MilkStash #BreastfeedingTips #PumpingMom #IBCLC #BreastfeedingJourney
Pin 4 — Breast Milk Storage Guide
How long does breast milk last?
✔ Up to 4 hours at room temperature
✔ Up to 4 days in the refrigerator
✔ Up to 6 months in the freezer
Knowing safe storage guidelines can help reduce waste and make feeding a little less stressful.
📌 Save this quick reference for later.

Pin 5 — Returning to Work While Breastfeeding
Heading back to work doesn't mean your breastfeeding journey has to end.
Planning ahead, pumping every few hours, and building a small milk stash can help make the transition feel more manageable.
📌 Save this checklist before your first day back at work.

If you’re building your baby registry, you’ve probably considered both:

标题：Postpartum Anxiety & Pumping Pressure | Mom Truths 101
描述：“I thought I was messing everything up.”

Seven months after welcoming her baby boy, Jessica looks back on the physical and emotional realities of her journey into motherhood.

In this episode of Mom Truths 101, she opens up about the sciatic pain she experienced during pregnancy, the pressure she placed on herself to pump eight times a day, and the postpartum anxiety that left her struggling to sleep, eat, and trust herself as a new mom.

When pumping, holding her baby, and constantly washing parts became too much, support from her family—and tools that fit her real life—helped her find a routine that worked for both her and her baby.

Looking back, Jessica would remind herself to take a deep breath, give herself grace, and remember that a crying baby does not mean she is doing something wrong.

To every mom who feels overwhelmed: you are learning, you are trying, and you are doing more than you realize. You don’t have to do it all perfectly—or alone.

We are told that a mother's love is endlessly patient and constantly fulfilled. But no one warns you about the quiet, heavy moments—when your arms ache from rocking a crying baby, and a fleeting, desperate thought whispers, “I can’t do this anymore.”
And then, the crushing weight of the guilt arrives.

If you have ever sat in the dark wondering what kind of mother feels this way, please know you are not alone, and you are not broken. It’s called maternal ambivalence. It is the very real, very human experience of loving your child with your entire soul, while simultaneously feeling frustration, anger, or even a deep grief for your old life.

The opposite of love isn’t anger. Sometimes, frustration just means you are deeply invested, completely depleted, and giving everything you have. Love and resentment can share the same space. You are allowed to hold both the overwhelming love and the overwhelming hard.

If you've been carrying this silent guilt, take a deep breath and let it go today. What is one part of motherhood you wish people were more honest about?

When is your baby ready to sleep in their own room? 💤🤍
If you're dreaming of better sleep but wondering whether it's time to move your little one to the nursery, you're not alone!

The first 6 months are especially important for safe sleep. Room-sharing (with baby sleeping in their own crib or bassinet) is recommended for at least the first 6 months to help reduce SIDS risk.

After 6 months, consider these 4 questions before making the transition:
🛏️ Is room-sharing disrupting your sleep?
🌙 How much help does your baby need overnight?
🏡 Is life relatively settled for your family?
👶 Can you still respond reliably to your baby's needs?

There's no one-size-fits-all timeline. Your family's sleep, routine, and ability to respond all matter. And wherever your baby sleeps, keep following safe sleep guidelines.

✨ Save this post for when you're considering the nursery transition, and share it with a parent navigating those sleepless nights!

Educational content only, not medical advice. Consult your healthcare provider for guidance tailored to your baby.

Katie Kim, a pediatric DNP & IBCLC, explains why it helps to plan ahead. 🤍

👶 Babies can get their first flu shot at 6 months old. Flu vaccination is recommended every year.

“Can I still breastfeed if I have the flu?” 🤒🍼
Katie Kim, a pediatric DNP & IBCLC, breaks it down: yes—in most cases, you can. 🤍
Flu doesn’t spread through breast milk. Your milk contains antibodies and other immune-supporting factors that can help protect your baby.

But flu can spread through close contact, so a few precautions matter:
✋️ Wash your hands before touching baby or pumping, and clean pump parts properly.
😷 Consider wearing a mask during close contact to help reduce the spread.
🍼 Too wiped out to nurse? If you’re able, express milk and have a healthy caregiver handle the feed while you rest.
💊 Taking medication? Check with your healthcare provider or pharmacist that it’s compatible with breastfeeding.
You deserve care, too. Rest when you can, and let someone lend a hand. 

Save this for sick days, and share it with a breastfeeding parent who needs the reassurance.

Is the flu shot really safe for babies? 🤔💉
Short answer: Yes.

For babies, the injectable flu vaccine uses inactivated virus or viral proteins—it can’t cause flu illness.

Mild side effects can happen, like:
• A sore, red, or swollen arm
• Feeling tired or fussy
• A low-grade fever
These usually pass quickly. If your child has a severe reaction or you’re concerned about their symptoms, contact your healthcare provider.

The flu vaccine isn’t guaranteed to prevent every infection, but it helps protect against serious flu complications. 🤍
